title: Who May Dwell on Your Holy Mountain?

verses.text: O LORD, who may abide in Your tent? Who may dwell on Your holy mountain?
He who walks with integrity and practices righteousness, who speaks the truth from his heart,
who has no slander on his tongue, who does no harm to his neighbor, who casts no scorn on his friend,
who despises the vile but honors those who fear the LORD, who does not revise a costly oath,
who lends his money without interest and refuses a bribe against the innocent. He who does these things will never be shaken.

context.author: The title says “of David” (Hebrew le-David), which can mean by David, for David or about David. Seventy-three psalms carry his name; tradition and the New Testament take many of them as his.
context.genre: Psalm: a song or prayer in Hebrew poetry
context.audience: Israel at worship in Jerusalem, and every reader who prays
context.setting: “O LORD, who may abide in Your tent? Who may dwell on Your holy mountain?” (v.1). The answer is a portrait of a person of integrity: “He who walks with integrity and practices righteousness, who speaks the truth from his heart” (v.2). He does not slander or harm his neighbor (v.3), honors those who fear the LORD, and “does not revise a costly oath” (v.4). He lends without interest and will not take a bribe against the innocent (v.5). “He who does these things will never be shaken” (v.5).
context.custom: Worshipers coming up to the sanctuary may have asked at the gate who could enter, and priests answered with the conditions, as in Psalm 24:3-6. God’s “tent” recalls the tabernacle where the ark stayed before the Temple was built (2 Samuel 6:17). The law forbade charging interest to a poor fellow Israelite (Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:35-37).
context.timelineImmediate: Psalm 16 delights in the LORD as “my chosen portion and my cup.”
context.timelineBible: Isaiah 33:14-16 asks the same question and gives a similar answer. Jesus taught, “Lend to them, expecting nothing in return” (Luke 6:35), and “Let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’” (Matthew 5:37), keeping one’s word.

translation.meaning: Tent, tabernacle. The tent of meeting where God dwelt among Israel.
Complete, whole, blameless; used of unblemished sacrifices.
Interest on a loan, literally “a bite.”

gospelParallels.note: Pursue holiness, without which no one will see the Lord.

otBackground.note: Who may ascend the hill of the LORD?
Who of us can dwell with consuming fire?
Do not charge interest to the poor.

overview.summary: Who may live with God? The one who walks with integrity, speaks truth, keeps his word and lends without exploiting; he will never be shaken.
overview.settingLine: At the gate of God’s holy mountain.

history.t: David housed the ark in a tent.
Questions and answers at the sanctuary gate.

customs.t: A promise kept even when it costs.

archaeology.t: Ancient Near Eastern loan contracts often charged 20-33 percent interest.
City gates at Dan and Bethsaida had small cult places.

overview.discussion: This person keeps a costly oath (v.4). Is there a promise I am tempted to revise because it now costs me more?
overview.book: The book of Psalms · 150 psalms (1-100 in the app so far). Israel’s songs and prayers: praise, lament, thanks, trust and wisdom, many of them by David.
overview.author: David
